procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated September 6, 1965 of the Patna High Court in Government Appeal No. 23 of 1962, setting aside the order of acquittal passed by the Second Additional Sessions Judge, Muzaffarpur, and convicting the appellant for an offence under s. 467, read with s. 109, IPC., and passing a sentence of three months' rigorous imprisonment.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The State of Bihar appealed the acquittal by the Sessions Judge to the Patna High Court. The High Court set aside the acquittal of the appellant and convicted him.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the High Court's order.

decision.appeal_result: In the result, the appeal is allowed.
decision.conviction_status: the order of the Second Additional Sessions Jndge, Muzaffarpur,_ acquitting the appellant, will stand restored.
decision.sentence_status: the order, under attack, is set aside

issue.issue_text: Whether the burden of proof can be shifted to the accused to support their defense plea, and whether their failure to produce evidence can be a basis for conviction.

facts: An appellant, acquitted by a trial court, was convicted by the High Court on appeal by the State.
The High Court's conviction was based on two main grounds:
1. The appellant raised a defense plea (that he attested loan applications on another's assurance) but did not produce any evidence to support it.
2. A co-accused with a similar defense did not testify on his own behalf under s. 342A of the Criminal Procedure Code, and the High Court applied this failure to the appellant's case as well.
law: In a criminal case, the burden of proof is on the prosecution to prove its case; it cannot be shifted to the accused.

Under the proviso to Section 342A of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.), the failure of an accused to give evidence shall not be the subject of any comment by the court, nor can it give rise to any presumption against the accused.
application: The Supreme Court found that by requiring the appellant to produce evidence in support of his plea, the High Court had incorrectly shifted the burden of proof onto him. The proper course was for the High Court to determine if the prosecution had proven its case and if the initial acquittal was erroneous.

The Supreme Court also found that the High Court committed a clear legal error by commenting on the failure of the accused (and his co-accused) to testify. This action was a direct breach of the specific prohibition in s. 342A of the Cr.P.C., which forbids the court from making such comments or drawing negative presumptions from an accused's silence.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's reasoning, holding that a conviction cannot be based on an accused's failure to produce evidence for their defense, as this improperly shifts the burden of proof from the prosecution. Furthermore, it is illegal for a court to comment on or draw an adverse inference from an accused's decision not to testify.

issue.issue_text: Whether a court can comment on the failure of an accused to examine themselves as a witness under Section 342A of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

facts: The appellant and a co-accused (Devendra Prasad) were acquitted by the Sessions Judge.
The State appealed to the High Court, which overturned the acquittal and convicted the appellant.
One of the High Court's reasons for conviction was that the co-accused, Devendra Prasad, had not examined himself as a witness under Section 342A of the Cr.P.C. to support his plea.
The High Court then stated that the "same consideration applied to the appellant also," effectively commenting on the appellant's failure to testify.
law: The Supreme Court cited the proviso to Section 342A of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.).
This proviso, specifically clause (b), states that the failure of an accused to give evidence "shall not be made the subject of any comment, by any of the parties, or the Court."
The law also prohibits such a failure from giving rise to "any presumption against himself, or any person charged, together with him."
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had committed a clear breach of the proviso to Section 342A.
By commenting on the co-accused's failure to testify and then applying that same reasoning to the appellant, the High Court illegally made the appellant's silence a subject of comment.
Furthermore, the High Court drew an adverse presumption against the appellant from this failure to testify, which is also explicitly forbidden by the statute.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's reasoning, holding that it is illegal for a court to comment on an accused's failure to examine themselves as a witness. Such a comment, and any presumption drawn from it, is a direct violation of the specific prohibition contained in the proviso to Section 342A of the Cr.P.C.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the burden of proof can be shifted to the accused to support their defense plea, and whether their failure to produce evidence can be a basis for conviction.
appellant_arguments: The High Court wrongly threw the burden of proof onto the appellant to prove their defense.
The conviction should not be based on the appellant's failure to produce evidence for their plea.
The primary duty is on the prosecution to prove its case, not on the accused to disprove it.
respondent_arguments: The appellant raised a specific defense that they acted on the assurance of a co-accused.
Since the appellant raised this defense, they had an obligation to produce some evidence to support it.
The failure to let in any evidence to support the defense plea was a valid ground for setting aside the acquittal and convicting the appellant.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a court can comment on the failure of an accused to examine themselves as a witness under Section 342A of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
appellant_arguments: The High Court's comment on the failure of the co-accused (and by extension, the appellant) to give evidence under s. 342A Cr.P.C. is illegal.
Drawing an adverse presumption from the failure to testify is a breach of the proviso to s. 342A.
The proviso to s. 342A explicitly prohibits the court from commenting on an accused's failure to give evidence or using it to form a presumption against them.
respondent_arguments: The failure of the co-accused, whose case was closely connected to the appellant's, to examine himself as a witness in support of his plea was a relevant consideration.
The court was justified in noting this failure when evaluating the credibility of the defense pleas raised by the accused.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The burden of proof is on the prosecution to prove its case, and a conviction cannot be based on an accused's failure to produce evidence in support of their defense plea. Furthermore, under the proviso to Section 342A of the Criminal Procedure Code, the failure of an accused to give evidence shall not be the subject of any comment by the court, nor shall it give rise to any adverse presumption against the accused.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court's order could not be sustained because it committed two serious errors. First, it improperly threw the burden of proof on the appellant to prove his defense, instead of first determining whether the prosecution had proven its case and whether the trial court's acquittal was erroneous. Second, it committed a breach of the proviso to Section 342A of the Criminal Procedure Code by commenting on the failure of a co-accused to examine himself as a witness and using that failure to draw an adverse presumption against the appellant.
legal_tests_applied: The primary duty is on the prosecution to prove its case, and the burden of proof cannot be thrown on the accused to support a defense plea as a basis for conviction.

Under the proviso to Section 342A of the Criminal Procedure Code, the failure of an accused to give evidence shall not be made the subject of any comment by the court, nor can it give rise to any presumption against the accused or any person charged together with him.
policy_considerations: The failure of an accused to produce evidence in support of his plea cannot be made the basis of a conviction, as it is for the prosecution to prove its case.

The statutory prohibition against commenting on an accused's failure to testify protects against adverse presumptions being drawn from the exercise of the right to remain silent, safeguarding both the individual accused and any co-accused in the same trial.
